sentences: A woman in a yellow jeogori, the traditional Korean jacket, fills the canvas from the waist up.
Kim Jong-tae painted it in oil in 1929, a brief, bright portrait where yellow meets red.
The canvas is modest, just 52 centimetres tall.
At the upper left, the year and the painter's name are written vertically.
Kim Jong-tae, who also went by the name Hoesan, was born in Gimpo, trained as a teacher and painted while teaching at a primary school in Seoul.
Behind her on the left, something like a wooden frame leans at an angle, perhaps a prop in the studio.
Its brown diagonals add depth, and the dull ochre wall behind quietly echoes the yellow of her jacket.
Look at her face.
Her gaze turns slightly to the right, and her firmly closed lips and bright eyes are caught in just a few quick, bold strokes.
A soft touch of pink on her cheeks gives the face its warmth.
The black cloth behind her works like a stage curtain, lifting her face and jacket forward.
Against the dark ground the yellow glows even brighter, and her black hair melts into the cloth so that only her face stays bright.
Now move down to the red collar and ties.
Below the white inner collar, the red band forms a V, and the long ties hang down, clashing boldly with the yellow.
This red band holds the composition firmly together.
Look closely at the sleeve on the right: the paint is so thin that the weave of the canvas shows through.
Washes as thin as ink and single sweeping strokes mark his style, recalling the brushwork of East Asian ink painting.
Because he chose to omit detail and use strong colour, he is often compared with the Fauves and the Expressionists.
Yet his simple poses and single-stroke touch are seen as entirely his own.
In 1936 the painter-critic Kim Yong-jun wrote that the picture showed a clear wish to capture a flavour unique to Korea.
He meant its pure, bright colours, which Koreans were thought to love.
Kim first had a work accepted at the Joseon Art Exhibition in 1926, then won its special prize again and again.
He died suddenly of illness in 1935, still in his twenties, while holding a solo show in Pyongyang.
So few of his works survive that this one, now in Korea's National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, has come to stand for his whole art.
Step back and imagine the yellow without those red ties.
